procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 02.03.2022 of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in CRR No.452 of 2021.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent No. 2 filed a Revision (CRR No.452 of 2021) before the Punjab & Haryana High Court challenging the Trial Court's order to summon Respondent No. 2 as an additional accused under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court allowed the Revision and set aside the Trial Court's order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant/Complainant approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court dated 02.03.2022, directing the trial to proceed in accordance with law.

directions: The order of the High Court dated 02.03.2022, is hereby set aside.
It is further directed that the trial shall proceed now in accordance with law, as expeditiously as possible.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside an order summoning an additional accused under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, by appreciating the merits of the evidence at the summoning stage, particularly considering that the accused was found innocent during investigation and had allegedly fled the spot.

facts: An informant (PW-9) filed an FIR naming three individuals as assailants, but they were not included in the charge-sheet, with one being found innocent during the investigation.
During the trial, the informant (PW-9), an eyewitness, testified in his examination-in-chief and identified the three individuals as being part of the crime.
Based on this testimony, the Trial Court allowed an application under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. and summoned the three individuals as additional accused.

The High Court, in a revision petition, set aside the Trial Court's order. Its reasoning was that one of the accused was found innocent during the investigation and had allegedly fled the spot without using a weapon.
law: Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. allows a court to summon a person not named as an accused if it appears from the evidence during the trial that they have committed an offence.
The standard for summoning under Section 319 is higher than a prima facie case for framing charges but short of the satisfaction required for a conviction. It requires strong evidence of complicity.
The merits of the evidence, including detailed examination and cross-examination of witnesses, are to be appreciated during the trial, not at the preliminary stage of a Section 319 application.
Under Section 149 of the IPC (unlawful assembly), a person's mere membership in the assembly is sufficient to attract liability; a specific individual role or overt act is not material.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed a grave error by appreciating the merits of the evidence at the summoning stage, which is impermissible.

The High Court's reliance on the fact that the accused was found innocent during the investigation was incorrect, as the court's power under Section 319 is triggered by evidence that emerges *during the trial*.

The Supreme Court noted that the High Court's observation about the accused fleeing was factually incorrect, as the eyewitness (PW-9) testified that the accused fled *after* the crime was committed by the unlawful assembly.

Furthermore, the Court held that since one of the charges was under Section 149 IPC, the accused's individual act (or lack thereof) was not the primary consideration. His presence as part of the unlawful assembly was sufficient for the Trial Court to be satisfied that he should be summoned.
The testimony of the eyewitness (PW-9) was considered sufficient evidence for the Trial Court to exercise its discretion under Section 319 and summon the additional accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning, holding that it was not justified in setting aside the summoning order. The High Court erred by prematurely evaluating the merits of the evidence and misapplying the law regarding unlawful assembly. The Supreme Court, therefore, set aside the High Court's order and restored the Trial Court's decision to summon the additional accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether, for the purpose of summoning an accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. for an offence involving Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, it is necessary to establish a specific individual role or act, or is being part of the unlawful assembly sufficient.

facts: An eyewitness (PW-9) testified in court and identified three additional persons as assailants who were involved in the crime.
These individuals were named in the initial police report (FIR) but were not formally charged by the police.
Based on the eyewitness testimony, the Trial Court summoned these three individuals to face trial under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).

The High Court overturned the Trial Court's order, reasoning that one of the summoned persons was found innocent during the initial investigation and had allegedly fled the scene without committing a specific act.
law: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), a person can be held criminally liable simply by being a member of an unlawful assembly. It is not necessary to prove that the individual committed a specific overt act.
The presence of an accused as part of an unlawful assembly is sufficient for a conviction under Section 149 IPC.
Section 319 Cr.P.C. allows a court to summon an additional accused during a trial if it appears from the evidence that this person has committed an offence.

The standard for summoning under Section 319 Cr.P.C. is more than a prima facie case (as needed for framing charges) but short of the level of proof required for a conviction. The court should not conduct a detailed examination of the evidence's merits at this stage.
application: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was wrong to analyze the merits of the evidence at the summoning stage. This task is reserved for the full trial.

The Court emphasized that since the charges included Section 149 IPC, the High Court failed to appreciate its legal requirements. For this offence, the key factor is membership in the unlawful assembly, not a specific individual role or act.

The eyewitness testimony of PW-9, which implicated the three individuals as being part of the unlawful assembly, was considered strong enough evidence to justify summoning them under Section 319 Cr.P.C.
The High Court's reasoning that one person fled the scene was dismissed, as the evidence suggested he fled *after* the crime was committed by the unlawful assembly he was part of.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view and held that for summoning an accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. for an offence involving Section 149 IPC, it is not necessary to establish a specific individual role or act. Being identified as a member of the unlawful assembly through evidence presented at trial is sufficient. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and reinstated the Trial Court's decision to summon the additional accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside an order summoning an additional accused under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, by appreciating the merits of the evidence at the summoning stage, particularly considering that the accused was found innocent during investigation and had allegedly fled the spot.
appellant_arguments: The trial court was correct to summon the additional accused based on the evidence of a witness (PW-9) that emerged during the trial.
The prosecution had fully made out its case for summoning the accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C.
The High Court committed a grave error by appreciating the merits of the evidence and allowing the revision, which is improper at the summoning stage.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's decision was correct as the accused was found innocent during the initial investigation.
The material on record was insufficient to summon the accused, as it could not be established that he was attributed any specific injury.
According to the complainant's own version, the accused had fled the spot, which supports his non-involvement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether, for the purpose of summoning an accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. for an offence involving Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, it is necessary to establish a specific individual role or act, or is being part of the unlawful assembly sufficient.
appellant_arguments: The evidence of the witness (PW-9) was sufficient to establish the accused's presence and involvement as part of the unlawful assembly, making it necessary for the trial court to summon him to face trial.
respondent_arguments: A specific role or act must be established to summon an accused, as it could not be established that the accused was attributed any specific injury.
The accused's act of fleeing the spot, as stated by the complainant, indicates a lack of participation in any specific criminal act.

cases.case_name: Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab and Others
cases.principle: Section 319 CrPC springs out of the doctrine judex damnatur cum nocens absolvitur (Judge is condemned when guilty is acquitted).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power to summon an additional accused under Section 319 of the Criminal Procedure Code is to be exercised when the prosecution has made out a prima facie case from the evidence presented, and not on a detailed evaluation of the evidence's credibility or an assessment of the probable actions of the accused, as that is a matter for trial.
obiter: Section 319 CrPC springs out of the doctrine judex damnatur cum nocens absolvitur (Judge is condemned when guilty is acquitted).

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed a grave error by appreciating the merits of the evidence at the summoning stage and setting aside the trial court's order. The trial court was absolutely correct to summon the additional accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. based on the eyewitness testimony of PW-9 that emerged during the trial, as the court had no alternative but to act on this new evidence.
legal_tests_applied: Under Sub-section (1) of Section 319 Cr.P.C., a court has the judicial discretion to summon a person as an accused if, during the trial, evidence appears before it indicating that such a person has committed an offence for which they should be tried together with the other accused.
why_respondent_won: The High Court committed a grave error by improperly appreciating the merits of the evidence at the summoning stage, which is not permissible.

The High Court's reasoning, which questioned the probability of an armed person fleeing without firing a shot and concluded this pointed to false implication, was an incorrect evaluation of evidence that should be reserved for trial.
The trial court was correct and had no alternative but to summon the accused persons once new evidence, in the form of an eyewitness (PW-9) statement, appeared before it during the trial.

The fact that the accused was found innocent during the investigation or allegedly fled the scene does not bar the trial court from exercising its power under Section 319 Cr.P.C. when sufficient evidence emerges during the trial.
policy_considerations: It is the duty of the court to do justice by punishing the real culprit. Where the investigating agency for any reason does not array one of the real culprits as an accused, the court is not powerless in calling the said accused to face trial.
